passage:
Sahil: Account's nearly empty and it's only the 26th??
Tanvir: How? Rent, groceries and the phone bill are all paid. Nothing big happened.
Sahil: I checked. No big charges at all.
Tanvir: The office snacks, the late-night orders, the cab when it rained...
Sahil: Those are like a hundred rupees each. That's nothing.
Tanvir: Maybe nothing times forty is something.
Sahil: I never wrote any of it down.
Tanvir: Neither did I. Each one felt too small to count.
Sahil: So where did it go?
Tanvir: I honestly don't know. I never counted them.
Sahil: Same. 😕

qa.q: What day of the month is it when Sahil notices the account is nearly empty?
What does Sahil's "??" after the 26th suggest about how Sahil feels?
qa.a: It suggests Sahil feels shocked and worried, since nothing big seems to explain the empty account.

qa.q: What could they do to find out where the money goes?
qa.a: For a few weeks they could note every purchase, even the small ones, to see what adds up.

qa.q: How might Tanvir be feeling as the conversation ends?
qa.a: Tanvir seems puzzled and a little guilty, since neither of them counted the small things.

grounding: Sahil and Tanvir never count small daily purchases, and at month end the account is short and neither can say where the money went.

passage:
In Hosur, Ira and Vaibhav both worked at the same electronics unit and rode home together on his bike. On the way there was a tea stall, then a bakery, then the phone recharge shop. A chai here, egg puffs there, and most nights a small online order of phone covers or hair clips. "It's only thirty rupees," Ira would say, and each time she was right.
On the 24th the landlord's rent reminder came, and their joint account didn't have enough. They sat on the steps of their rented room, scrolling through the bank app.
"Where did it go?" Vaibhav asked. "We didn't buy anything big."
Ira scrolled and scrolled through tiny entries. "We didn't buy anything big," she repeated slowly. Neither of them could say what the month had been spent on.

qa.q: What would Ira say about each small purchase?
How did Ira feel as she repeated "We didn't buy anything big"?
qa.a: She was confused and uneasy, starting to see that the many tiny entries had added up.

qa.q: What could the couple try next month?
qa.a: They could note every small purchase for a few weeks so they can see where the money goes before deciding what to change.

qa.q: What would have changed if they had counted the chai and puffs from the start?
qa.a: They would have seen the small daily costs adding up well before the 24th, instead of being caught short on rent.

grounding: It shows a couple who never count daily snacks and small online orders finding the account short at month end with no idea where the money went.

passage:
Soo-ah and Jana shared a flat in Leipzig and a joint account for food and household things. Neither of them ever logged the small stuff: a pastry from the bakery on the way to the tram, a two-euro phone game, a late-night grocery delivery "just for milk", a candle from the market. Each thing was too small to count.
On 28 March the joint card was declined at the supermarket checkout with a queue behind them. Jana went red. Outside, they opened the banking page on Soo-ah's phone and scrolled. Pages of tiny amounts, most of which neither of them could remember.
"We didn't go on holiday. We didn't buy a sofa," Soo-ah said. "So where did it all go?"
Jana just shook her head. Neither of them could explain the month.

qa.q: When was the joint card declined?
qa.a: On 28 March, at the supermarket checkout.

qa.q: Why did Jana go red at the checkout?
qa.a: Jana felt embarrassed with a queue behind them and shocked that the card had been declined.

qa.q: What could Soo-ah and Jana try next month?
qa.a: They could log every small purchase on the joint account for a few weeks and look at the total together each Sunday.

qa.q: What is it like for Soo-ah scrolling through the pages of tiny amounts?
qa.a: Soo-ah is baffled and a little alarmed, because nothing big was bought and yet the money is gone.

grounding: It shows flatmates who never count small purchases finding the joint account short at month end and unable to explain where the money went.
